question: What happened when Bordeaux oenology students were given a white wine dyed red to smell, and why did they describe it with red-wine words?

facts.fact: The study "The Color of Odors" was published in the journal Brain and Language in 2001.
facts.quote: Brain and Language 79, 309–320 (2001)

facts.fact: The paper was published online on August 28, 2001.
facts.quote: Published online August 28, 2001

facts.fact: Its authors were Gil Morrot of INRA Montpellier, and Frédéric Brochet and Denis Dubourdieu of the Faculty of Oenology at the University of Bordeaux 2.
facts.quote: Frédéric Brochet and Denis Dubourdieu

facts.fact: Brochet did the work towards a doctorate at the Faculty of Oenology in Bordeaux.
facts.quote: following work carried out towards a doctorate from the Faculty of Oenology

facts.fact: The study began by analysing the written tasting notes of four wine experts.
facts.quote: Our study first focuses on the influence of vision on smell by carrying out a lexical analysis of four wine experts’ tasting comments.

facts.fact: One of the four sets of tasting notes was 7,000 comments written by Robert Parker for The Wine Advocate.
facts.quote: The 7000 tasting comments were written by Robert Parker.

facts.fact: The analysis found that experts mostly describe a wine's smell with objects that are the same colour as the wine.
facts.quote: The analysis shows that the odors of a wine are, for the most part, represented by objects that have the color of the wine.

facts.fact: That pattern is why the researchers suspected that a wine's colour steers how people name its smell.
facts.quote: Evidence of the relationship between the perceived odor and the color of a wine initially led us to hypothesize that the color of a wine directs the identification of its odor.

facts.fact: The test used two 1996 Bordeaux wines, a white made from sémillon and sauvignon and a red made from cabernet-sauvignon and merlot.
facts.quote: containing sémillon and sauvignon grapes for the white wine (wine W), and cabernet-sauvignon and merlot grapes for the red wine (wine R).

facts.fact: The wines were 1996 vintage.
facts.quote: vintage 1996

facts.fact: Part of the white wine was dyed red with 2 grams per litre of purified grape anthocyanins, the natural red pigment of grapes.
facts.quote: Part of the white wine was colored red (wine RW) with 2 g/L of purified grape anthocyanins

facts.fact: To check that the dye had no smell, 50 people recruited on the ENSIA Massy campus compared the dyed and plain white wine in opaque glasses.
facts.quote: The neutrality test of the dye was carried out by 50 people recruited on the ENSIA Massy campus.

facts.fact: Those tests showed the dyed and plain white wine smelled the same, so the dye was judged odourless.
facts.quote: It is therefore concluded that wines W and RW are perceived as identical and that the dye can be regarded as having no odor.

facts.fact: The tasters were 54 undergraduates from the Faculty of Oenology of the University of Bordeaux.
facts.quote: The wine comparison test was carried out by 54 undergraduates from the Faculty of Oenology of the University of Bordeaux.

facts.fact: The tasting was done in two sessions one week apart.
facts.quote: The wine comparison test was carried out in two sessions separated by 1 week.

facts.fact: The wines were served in clear glasses under white light, so the tasters could see the colour.
facts.quote: The wines were presented in clear AFNOR glasses, under artificial white lighting.

facts.fact: In the first session the students wrote a list of smell words for the real white wine and the real red wine.
facts.quote: During first session, the subjects were requested to draw up a list of odor descriptors for wine W and R.

facts.fact: In the first session they described the red with red or dark objects and the white with yellow or clear objects.
facts.quote: During the first session, the subjects chose odors represented by red or dark objects to describe wine R and yellow or clear objects to describe wine W.

facts.fact: Red-wine smell words the students used included blackcurrant.
facts.quote: cassis (blackcurrant)

facts.fact: Red-wine smell words the students used included raspberry.
facts.quote: framboise (raspberry)

facts.fact: White-wine smell words the students used included honey.
facts.quote: miel (honey)

facts.fact: White-wine smell words the students used included lychee.
facts.quote: litchi (lychee)

facts.fact: In the second session the two glasses were the white wine and the same white wine dyed red.
facts.quote: The two wines then proposed were W and RW.

facts.fact: In the second session each student got back their own list of words, in alphabetical order, with no hint of which wine each had gone with.
facts.quote: For the second session, each subject received his/her own list of descriptors, from the first session, given in alphabetical order and without indications concerning the wines.

facts.fact: The students generally used the words they had used for the real red wine to describe the dyed white wine.
facts.quote: During the second session, the subjects generally used the odor descriptors they had used to characterize wine R to describe the wine RW.

facts.fact: For the dyed wine they also dropped the words they had used for the white wine.
facts.quote: Moreover, in their olfactory description of wine RW, they eliminated the descriptors they had used for wine W.

facts.fact: The authors conclude that what the tasters saw overrode what they smelled.
facts.quote: Hence, because of the visual information, the tasters discounted the olfactory information.

facts.fact: The authors call the effect a real perceptual illusion.
facts.quote: The observed phenomenon is a real perceptual illusion.

facts.fact: In a separate test, Brochet served the same red Bordeaux to 57 people a week apart under two labels, one suggesting a table wine and one a prestigious wine.
facts.quote: the same red Bordeaux superior wine was presented to 57 subjects at an interval of one week and under two very different labels.

facts.fact: Brochet's dissertation was titled "Taste: A Study in the Representation of Chemical Substances in the Arena of Consciousness."
facts.quote: a doctoral dissertation entitled “Taste: A Study in the Representation of Chemical Substances in the Arena of Consciousness.”

facts.fact: Brochet submitted the work to the Académie Amorim prize run by a Portuguese cork maker, and it took the runner-up position for 2001.
facts.quote: But Brochet’s little bombshell took runner-up position

facts.fact: Afterwards the London Times reported the work as proof that wine experts know no more than anyone else.
facts.quote: wine ‘experts’ know no more than the rest of us.

facts.fact: Wikipedia summarises the study as 54 undergraduate oenology students at the University of Bordeaux tasting two glasses in 2001.
facts.quote: In 2001, researchers from the University of Bordeaux asked 54 undergraduate oenology students to test two glasses of wine: one red, one white.

people.name: Frédéric Brochet
people.role: Doctoral researcher at the Faculty of Oenology, University of Bordeaux 2; co-author of the dye study and author of the label study
people.stake: His doctorate, and a finding that questioned how much wine tasters' words come from the wine itself; the work drew press mockery of wine experts and placed runner-up for the 2001 Académie Amorim prize

people.name: Gil Morrot
people.role: Researcher at INRA Montpellier, first author and corresponding author of "The Color of Odors"
people.stake: Credit for showing that colour changes how people name smells

people.name: Denis Dubourdieu
people.role: Co-author, Faculty of Oenology, University of Bordeaux 2

people.name: The 54 oenology undergraduates
people.role: Students at the Faculty of Oenology in Bordeaux who did the tasting (unnamed)
people.stake: Their trained noses: in the second session they described a dyed white wine with the red-wine words they had used a week earlier

timeline.when: Before the tasting (years of notes; exact dates not given in the paper)
timeline.what: The team analysed thousands of tasting notes by four wine experts, including 7,000 by Robert Parker, and found smells were mostly named after objects the colour of the wine.
timeline.why: To study how tasters build their perception of wine from what they write down.

timeline.what: Part of a 1996 Bordeaux white wine was dyed red with grape anthocyanins, and 50 people at ENSIA Massy checked in opaque glasses that the dye had no smell.
timeline.why: The colour link in the notes made them suspect colour directs smell naming; the dye check made sure any change came from the colour alone.

timeline.what: 54 Bordeaux oenology undergraduates wrote smell words for a real white and a real red wine in clear glasses, using red or dark objects for the red and yellow or clear objects for the white.
timeline.why: To get each student's own vocabulary for a real red and a real white.

timeline.what: The same students got the white wine and the same white wine dyed red, plus their own word lists, and generally gave the dyed white the red-wine words while dropping its white-wine words.
timeline.why: To see whether colour alone would change which smell words they picked.

timeline.what: Morrot, Brochet and Dubourdieu published "The Color of Odors" in Brain and Language, calling the effect a real perceptual illusion.

Brochet's doctoral work, including a test where the same Bordeaux was served to 57 people under a cheap and a prestigious label, placed runner-up for the 2001 Académie Amorim prize, and the press ran it as proof wine experts know no more than anyone.

turn.what: In session 2 there was no red wine on the table at all, only the same white in two glasses, one dyed red with an odourless grape pigment; the students still described the red-looking glass with the red-wine words they had used a week earlier, so the 'smell' came from the colour.

key_objects: Two clear wine glasses side by side, one pale yellow and one red, holding the same white wine
A bottle of 1996 white Bordeaux (sémillon and sauvignon) and one of red Bordeaux (cabernet-sauvignon and merlot)
A small vial or dropper of red grape pigment (anthocyanins) being stirred into white wine
A tasting booth with a handwritten list of smell words: blackcurrant, raspberry versus honey, lychee
Opaque black tasting glasses (the dye check)
A calendar with two sessions one week apart
The journal page "The Color of Odors", Brain and Language, 2001
Two bottles with different labels: table wine versus prestigious wine (Brochet's label test)
unverified: "Wine experts" or "sommeliers" were fooled: the dye test was done by 54 undergraduates from the Faculty of Oenology, not experts or sommeliers. Only the earlier text analysis used experts' notes.

"They called the white wine red" / "they said it was a red wine": the students weren't asked the wine's colour. They picked which glass matched each of their smell words more strongly. The paper says they described its smell as a red wine's.
"Not one of them noticed" / "all 54": the paper says the students "generally" used the red-wine words. It gives no count of how many did or didn't.
"Jammy" and "crushed red fruit" (Wikipedia, citing the Guardian): these words aren't in the paper. Its descriptor list includes blackcurrant, raspberry, cherry, prune, spice and others.
"Fresh, dry, honeyed, lively" vs "intense, spicy, supple, deep" (Seattle Weekly): these aren't the descriptors in the published paper.
"Both glasses came from the same bottle" in a single tasting: in session 1 the red was a real, different red wine. Only in session 2, a week later, were both glasses the same white wine.
"The experiment happened in 2001": 2001 is the publication year. The paper doesn't say when the tastings were done.

"Tasteless dye" / "food colouring": the dye was purified grape anthocyanins (E 163). The paper's check, with 50 people, was for odour in opaque glasses. Brochet's essay says olfactory and taste neutrality were checked, but the paper reports only the odour result.
Brochet alone ran or published the study: the paper has three authors, and Gil Morrot (INRA Montpellier) is first author and corresponding author.
57 tasters: this number belongs to Brochet's separate label test, not the dye test (54).
Brochet "won" the Académie Amorim prize: Seattle Weekly says his work was runner-up. The 2001 grand prize went to a vine-genetics study.

The study proves wine tasting is fake or that experts can't tell red from white by smell: the paper reports a naming illusion when colour is visible. It notes that, in their own tests without sight, people judged red vs white correctly about 70% of the time (vs 50% chance).
The label test's quoted descriptors ("woody, complex, and round" vs "short, light, and faulty") come from Seattle Weekly's retelling. Brochet's essay gives its own word list.
